ground: "In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving." The ayah is a single noun phrase with no finite verb. The preposition bi- ("in / with / by") hangs on an unstated act, and that act is whatever is being begun, here the recitation of the surah itself. The name is God's (Allāh). Two adjectives from one root (r-ḥ-m, mercy) follow it: raḥmān, an intensive form used only of God, and raḥīm, a form the Quran also uses for the Prophet and the believers.

triggers.how: The classical entries derive ism from sumuww (height). Rāghib glosses it as 'that by which the essence of a thing is known'. Here B005 (naming) is joined with B001 (rising) and B002 (the raised figure that shows from afar, like the new moon's sumāwa over the horizon).
The name belongs to one who is not seen; the name is what appears of Him.

findings.statement: 'In the name of God' also holds the root's picture of a name as what rises and becomes visible from a distance: the part of the unseen God that stands up where a person can make it out and address it.
findings.perceptible: In Turkish, 'isim' is only a label. This finding makes the name spatial. It is the raised, visible outline by which something far off is recognised, so beginning 'in the name' means beginning under the one thing about God that is in view. That prepares the move from speaking about Him (1:1–4) to speaking to Him (1:5).

triggers.how: Shared scene. The rabb is the owner and master of the beast (plan I2).
Shared scene. The ḍālla is the beast left in the waste whose rabb is not known, i.e. the unmarked animal.
Sound and scene. Naʿam is the herd.
Scene. The hādī is the lead animal at the front of the herd.

findings.statement: Heard through the documented alternative derivation from wasm, 'in the name of God' can also sound like setting out under God's mark, the brand (sima) by which what is His is known. The plain sense of beginning with His name stays intact.
findings.perceptible: Starting in God's name becomes an act of belonging: being visibly His. This frames the surah between the mark in its first word and the stray in its last word, the beast whose owner no one can tell (1:7).

triggers.how: Concordance. The name is mentioned 'over what He provided them of the beasts of the herd (bahīmat al-anʿām)'. See also 22:28, 22:36, 6:118–121.
Naʿam is heard beside anʿām.

findings.statement: The Quran's commonest use of ism is the name that is mentioned or remembered (14 of 39 uses), several times the name spoken over herd animals. So the basmala's name is heard as something said over a thing, a mention that claims it for God.
findings.perceptible: This supports the brand image (F2) from inside the Quran's own usage. God's name is spoken over livestock the way a mark is put on them. The name is a word laid on something so that it is known as belonging to Him.

triggers.how: Concordance. The bi-smi phrase goes with boarding the ark and its sailing.
Concordance. The same phrase goes with the command to read or recite.
Concordance. The full formula heads Solomon's letter.

findings.statement: The phrase 'in the name of' has no verb of its own. It attaches to whatever act follows (reading, sailing, writing), so the reciter's own act fills the gap.
findings.perceptible: The basmala is incomplete until something is done. Here the act being done is this recitation, and every word after it is carried 'by' or 'with' the name the way the ark is carried in 11:41.

triggers.how: Same root, same branches, placed side by side.
Shared scene (kin.birth_nursing). The rabb is the fosterer who raises a child stage by stage.

findings.statement: 'The All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving' keeps in its root raḥim, the womb (B003) and the kinship that flows from it (B002). The mercy it names is heard as the tenderness (B001) of what holds something growing inside it.
findings.perceptible: Mercy becomes bodily and connected to kin instead of an abstract pity handed down from above. It is the care of an enclosing place toward what it holds and feeds, and the rabb who raises in 1:2 is heard inside that care.

triggers.how: The same two words repeat right after رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ.
Repetition.

findings.statement: The pair raḥmān–raḥīm appears here and again in 1:3, so the lordship named in 1:2 sits between two statements of mercy.
findings.perceptible: This is compositional. Rabb is enclosed by mercy on both sides, the way something is held in a womb, so lordship is not heard alone before the mention of the Day of Judgement (1:4).

triggers.how: The two patterns (faʿlān, faʿīl) come from the same root.

findings.statement: The entry says faʿlān is a pattern for intensive description and that raḥmān 'may not be said of other than God', the one 'whose mercy encompasses all things'. Abū ʿUbayda compares the pair to nadmān and nadīm.
findings.perceptible: Two words that Turkish hears as near-duplicates have different edges. Raḥmān is overflowing and belongs to God alone. Raḥīm is the form the Quran can also give to the Prophet (9:128) and to believers among themselves (48:29), i.e. mercy that can be shared and passed on.

triggers.how: Concordance. Walad (child) is a collocate. The Quran denies that ar-Raḥmān takes a child (19:88–92).
Concordance. Raḥmān is used as a name that people question.

findings.statement: Across the Quran, raḥmān works almost as a proper name (grammatical subject, the one seated on the Throne) and is repeatedly set against the claim that He has a child. So the womb in its root is heard as holding and tending, not as begetting.
findings.perceptible: This guards the womb image (F5) from inside the Quran. The mercy is womb-like in how it encloses and nourishes, and the same word is the one the Quran uses to deny God any offspring.

triggers.how: Shared scene (ritual.prayer / divine.lordship). Taʾalluh means worship; ilāh is what is made an object of worship.
The same name repeats.

findings.statement: The name Allāh sits in the same root family as ilāh, 'the one worshipped' (B001), and is also the name used in oath and direct address (B002: Allāhumma, yā Allāh). So the name at the head of the surah already contains the worship and the calling that 1:5 will state openly.
findings.perceptible: The word that Turkish hears only as a proper name carries the act the surah reaches in 1:5 ('You alone we serve'), and it is the form used to call on someone, which prepares the turn to 'You'.

triggers.how: Shared scene kin.birth_nursing. Raḥim (womb) sits next to walah (a mother parted from her child).
Same scene.

findings.statement: Under the documented alternative derivation from walah (distraught longing, B001; a mother made frantic by separation from her child, B002), the name heard beside the womb-mercy names can also carry the ache of one who longs toward what it is tied to.
findings.perceptible: Put next to raḥim, this completes a mother–child scene: the one who encloses, and the longing when separated. It gives the stray of 1:7 a pull toward return.

triggers.how: Shared scene (sign.marking / know.perceiving). ʿālam is a mark or sign.
know.perceiving

findings.statement: Through tawassum, reading a sign in someone's face, the name can also be heard as a sign for the one who looks, a mark from which the viewer reads the state of what it is on.
findings.perceptible: The name is something to be read as well as said. It joins the ʿālamīn of 1:2 (the worlds, heard also as marks and signs) as things in which the owner can be discerned.

triggers.how: Scene water.rain_cloud / plant.growth_decay. Also the Turkish reader hears rahmet as rain (memory).
Scene: growth, greenness, cloud.

findings.statement: Through al-wasmī, the first rain that 'marks the ground with plants', the opening name can also be heard as a first rain that leaves its mark in growth. The plain sense of beginning in God's name is untouched.
findings.perceptible: This is temporal and material. The first word of the book is heard as the season's first rain, and it leads into the rabb who makes things grow in 1:2.

triggers.how: Scenes dwelling.building (roof/pillar) and sky.bodies (zenith).
Scene dwelling.building (wall).

findings.statement: Samāʾ, 'whatever is above you and shades you', the roof of a house, shares the root of ism. So beginning in the name can also be heard as beginning under something that covers and shades from above.
findings.perceptible: The name becomes a canopy over the act. The surah opens under a roof, and walls (1:4) and a pillar that stands upright (1:6) follow.

triggers.how: Scene speech.praise_blame (boasting/praise).
Concordance. Names that people and their forefathers invented.

findings.statement: Musāmāt (rivalling someone's height or standing) and 'fulān lā yusāmā', 'he cannot be rivalled', live in the same root, so God's name can also be heard as the height no rival reaches.
findings.perceptible: This is relational. Among competing names, including the names of invented gods that the Quran dismisses, this is the name that cannot be competed with. That sets up praise belonging to God alone (1:2).

triggers.how: Praise is the spreading of good report.
Scene speech.news (message).

findings.statement: Samāh, a good reputation that spreads, belongs to the root, so the name can also be heard as God's fame for good, and the praise of 1:2 continues it.
findings.perceptible: Ism is heard as renown as well as a label: something carried outward by others' voices.

triggers.how: Scene body.illness (disease).
Same root.

findings.statement: The root also names the womb's ache after giving birth (raḥūm, B004), so the mercy names can carry, faintly, the cost borne by the one who has held and delivered.
findings.perceptible: This is bodily. Womb-mercy includes a pain taken on for the sake of the one born, not only softness.

triggers.how: Scene time.age (appointed time).
Scene ritual.sanctuary.

findings.statement: Mawsim, the marked season or gathering (the pilgrimage, the fairs), shares the wasm derivation, so the opening mark can also be heard as the marker of an appointed time when people gather.
findings.perceptible: This is temporal. Beginning is set against a fixed day toward which people assemble, and it points ahead to the Day in 1:4.

triggers.how: Scene hunt.chase (falcon).
Scene travel.open_land (waste, getting lost).

findings.statement: Samā l-qawm, going out into the empty wastes to hunt, belongs to the root, so the opening word can also be heard as setting out into open land.
findings.perceptible: The surah begins with going out and ends at the danger of being lost in the waste. The two ends are connected spatially.

triggers.how: Scene pastoral.breeding (newborn).

findings.statement: Samā l-faḥl, the stallion rising over and moving among the she-camels, belongs to the root. It is a herd picture next to the owner and the herd of I2.
findings.perceptible: It adds, minimally, the herd's own life under a strong one who rises over it. It does not join the brand image directly.

triggers.how: The entry cites the verse 'bi-smi lladhī fī kulli sūratin simuh' for the form sim/sum.

findings.statement: The dictionary shows the name in the variant forms sim and sum, in a verse about 'the name of the One whose name is in every surah'.
findings.perceptible: This records that the entry itself links the name with its place at the head of surahs. It adds no new sense.

loaded_words.role: The name as something mentioned or remembered (dhikr), often spoken over provision and herd animals; bi-smi goes with an act that is begun (reading, boarding, a letter).
loaded_words.count: 14 of 39 as the object of mention or remembrance; 4 of 39 in a bi-smi phrase
loaded_words.departure: The translation 'name' flattens it into a label. The recurring role is a name that is spoken over something and remembered, not just held as an identifier.

loaded_words.role: Works almost as a proper name for God: a grammatical subject, the one seated on the Throne, and repeatedly the one of whom a child is denied.
loaded_words.count: 57 of 57 of God; 16 as grammatical subject
loaded_words.departure: 'The Compassionate' makes it an adjective. In the Quran it acts as a name, and the entry says it may be said of no one but God.

loaded_words.role: Describes God, usually paired with ghafūr, tawwāb or raʾūf, and can be shared with the Prophet and the believers.
loaded_words.departure: Translations that treat it as a mere doubling of raḥmān lose that it is the form mercy takes when it can be passed on (9:128, 48:29).

loaded_words.role: The proper name, mostly as grammatical subject or topic, related to ilāh, 'the worshipped'.
loaded_words.count: 212 of 400 sampled as grammatical subject or topic
loaded_words.departure: Here it is the possessor of the name, not an actor. The name stands for the one who is not seen.

losses.loses: The height and visibility in the root (sumuww, a figure rising on the horizon), the canopy of samāʾ, good repute, and, through the alternative derivation, the owner's mark (wasm).
losses.adds: A grammatical sense (a part of speech) that the Arabic does not carry here.

losses.loses: The open verb slot. The phrase still needs an act to attach to; in Turkish it has become a set formula.
losses.adds: Everyday uses as an exclamation before eating or starting something, and as a startled cry to ward off fear or evil ('Bismillah!'). These make it sound like a protective charm.

losses.loses: How clearly it relates to ilāh, 'the worshipped', and to the form of calling on someone.
losses.adds: It is heard only as a proper name. It also appears in interjections ('Allah Allah') and oaths, which the Arabic shares.

losses.loses: Womb (raḥim) and kinship (B002, B003), and the difference between an intensive mercy belonging to God alone and a mercy that can be shared.
losses.adds: Use as men's personal names. Rahîm also sounds almost the same as the anatomical 'rahim', which Turkish treats as a separate word (the card marks it as a false friend), so the link the Arabic keeps is heard as an accident.

losses.loses: Bodily, kin-bound tenderness. Merhamet leans toward pity from above.
losses.adds: Rahmet also means rain in Turkish ('rahmet yağıyor') and is used of the dead ('rahmetli'). Merhamet adds a condescending pity.

losses.loses: The womb and kinship picture entirely. 'Esirgeyen' (sparing, protecting) keeps only the protective side.
losses.adds: 'Bağışlayan' brings in forgiveness (maghfira), which is not in r-ḥ-m.

grammar: The whole ayah is one genitive phrase with no verb. Bi- attaches to an unstated act, which is the reciter's act of starting (compare 96:1 iqraʾ bi-smi, 11:41 bi-smi llāhi majrāhā).
Bi- can be heard as 'with' (accompaniment) or 'by' (means). The name goes along with the act, and the act is carried out by means of it.

Raḥmān (faʿlān, intensive, said only of God) and raḥīm (faʿīl, a lasting quality the Quran also gives to the Prophet and believers) come from the same root in two different patterns. Turkish hears two near-synonyms.
reread: The surah begins with something that has not yet happened: 'in the name of' waits for an act, and the act is this recitation. The name is what rises into view of a God who is not seen, like a figure made out on the horizon. Heard through wasm, it is also the mark by which what belongs to Him is known, a name spoken over His own the way the Quran has it spoken over the herd. The one named is called by two words for mercy whose root is the womb, and which will wrap around the rabb of 1:2. So the belonging marked here is not branding by a stranger. It is the enclosing care of something that holds and feeds what grows inside it. The surah opens with this mark and closes, in 1:7, with the unmarked stray whose owner no one knows.

set_aside.what: و ل ه~alt B004 al-mūlah, the spider (animal.small, with مَٰلِكِ 'bee')
set_aside.why: Nothing in the ayah or the surah completes an image with it, and it contributes no picture to the plain reading of the name.

set_aside.what: و ل ه~alt B002 used as 'sale separation' and 'captive' (trade.sale, war.battle scenes)
set_aside.why: Separating mother and child in a sale or captivity is kept only as maternal separation next to the womb (F10). The market and war roles do not join any image activated in 1:1.

set_aside.what: و ل ه~alt B003 water sent into the desert and lost
set_aside.why: It touches 'vanishing' with ḍāllīn, but that link runs through the alternative root of a single name and adds nothing F18 and I2 do not already make perceptible. Noted here only.

set_aside.what: و س م~alt B005–B006 beauty (wasāma) and the dye plant wasma
set_aside.why: Beauty on a person, and a dye, have no member in the neighbourhood beyond the mechanical craft.dyeing pairing with ʿālamīn. The marking sense is already covered by F2 and F11.

set_aside.what: س م و B004 the horse's back as samāʾ (body.limbs)
set_aside.why: The 'back' role is mechanical. The canopy sense of samāʾ is kept in F13.
